about.title: How the script works
about.text:
Bengali is written from left to right. There are no capital letters. Most letters hang from a horizontal line along the top called the maatraa; a few letters (such as এ, ঐ, ও, ঙ, ঞ, ৎ) have no top line at all, and several (খ, গ, ণ, থ, ধ, প, শ) have a line with a gap in it - these gaps are part of the letter, not sloppy handwriting.

The script is not an alphabet in the English sense. Each consonant letter stands for a consonant plus a built-in vowel, so ক is not 'k' but 'ko'. To get a different vowel you attach a vowel sign to the consonant: কা kaa, কি ki, কে ke. A vowel has a full, independent letter only when it starts a word or follows another vowel: আম (aam, mango), but নাম (naam, name) with the sign.

A sentence ends with the daanri (।) instead of a full stop. The question mark, comma and exclamation mark are the same as in English.

The traditional order of the letters is scientific: vowels first, then consonants grouped by where in the mouth they are made, from the throat (ক) forward to the lips (ম). Learning them in rows of five makes the sounds much easier to remember.

examples.english: mango (independent vowel at the start of a word)
name (the same vowel as a sign after n)

about.title: The built-in vowel: o, and when it disappears
about.text:
The vowel built into every consonant is written অ when it stands alone. It is NOT the 'a' of Hindi or Sanskrit. It has two pronunciations: an open sound like the 'o' in British English 'hot', and a closed sound like the 'o' in 'go' said short and without gliding. This course writes both as o, because the difference never changes the meaning of the words taught here; copy the audio.

A rough guide: the closed 'o' is used when the next syllable has i or u (অতি oti, মধু modhu), before ক্ষ, জ্ঞ and a য-ফলা (লক্ষ lokkho, সত্য shotto), and at the end of a word. Elsewhere, especially in the first syllable, it is usually the open 'o' (গরম gorom, কলম kolom).

The hard part is knowing when the built-in vowel is silent, because the spelling does not show it.

1. At the end of a word it is usually silent: নাম is naam, not naamo; ফল is phol.

2. It IS pronounced at the end after a conjunct (গল্প golpo, শান্ত shaanto), in many common adjectives and number words (ছোট chhoto, বড় boro, কত koto, এত eto), and in verb endings (করব korbo, করল korlo, করত korto). Modern spelling often writes this final o openly with ো: ভালো bhaalo, এগারো egaaro, করো koro.

3. In the middle of a word it is often dropped to keep the rhythm: আমরা is aamraa, করতে is korte, জানলা is jaanlaa.

The romanisation in this course always shows what is actually said, so when in doubt, trust the roman line.

examples.english: hot (both o's are said; the built-in vowel of the final m is silent)
small (final o said, though not written)
good (final o written with a vowel sign)

about.title: Vowel signs
about.text:
Every vowel except অ has two shapes: a full letter, and a sign (called a kaar) that attaches to a consonant. The sign replaces the built-in o.

The signs do not all sit to the right of the consonant. আ-কার ( া ) goes on the right; ই-কার ( ি ) is written on the LEFT although it is spoken after the consonant; ঈ-কার ( ী ) goes on the right; উ, ঊ and ঋ signs hang below; এ-কার ( ে ) and ঐ-কার ( ৈ ) go on the left; ও-কার ( ো ) and ঔ-কার ( ৌ ) wrap around both sides. So কি is ki and কে is ke, even though the sign is written first.

A few consonant + vowel combinations have special shapes you simply have to recognise: গু (gu), রু (ru), রূ (roo), শু (shu), হু (hu), হৃ (hri).

Long and short: ই / ঈ and উ / ঊ were once short and long, but in modern Bengali both members of each pair sound the same. The spelling still matters (it is how you tell কি 'whether' from কী 'what'), and this course keeps it visible by writing i for ই and ee for ঈ, u for উ and oo for ঊ. Do not lengthen ee and oo as you would in English.

examples.english: (yes/no question word) - sign written on the left
the syllable ko - sign on both sides
teacher, guru (special shapes of gu and ru)

about.title: Breathy and plain consonants
about.text:
Bengali consonants come in pairs: a plain one and an aspirated one said with a strong puff of breath - ক k / খ kh, গ g / ঘ gh, চ ch / ছ chh, জ j / ঝ jh, ট t / ঠ th, ড d / ঢ dh, ত t / থ th, দ d / ধ dh, প p / ফ ph, ব b / ভ bh.

The difference changes meaning, so it must be heard and made. English k, t, p at the start of a word are already slightly breathy; the Bengali plain ক, ত, প have NO puff (like the k in 'sky', the t in 'stop', the p in 'spin'), and খ, থ, ফ have much more.

In the romanisation, h after a consonant always means this puff of breath. So th is never the English 'th' of 'think', and ph is not necessarily 'f' (though many speakers do say ফ as f, and ভ close to v). The pair written ch / chh is চ / ছ: ch is like the ch in 'church' without breath, chh the same with breath.

about.title: Two kinds of t and d, and two kinds of r
about.text:
Bengali has two rows of t/d sounds. The dental row - ত থ দ ধ ন - is made with the tip of the tongue touching the back of the upper teeth (like t and d in Spanish or Italian). The retroflex row - ট ঠ ড ঢ ণ - is made with the tongue tip further back, on the ridge behind the teeth, and sounds close to the English t and d. English words borrowed into Bengali are therefore spelt with the retroflex letters: টেবিল (table), ডাক্তার (doctor).

This course does NOT mark the difference in the romanisation: both ত and ট are written t, both দ and ড are d. That keeps the roman line easy to read, but it means you must learn this distinction from the Bengali spelling and the audio. Pairs such as সাত shaat (seven) and ষাট shaat (sixty) differ only in the kind of t.

There are also two r sounds. র is a light tap of the tongue. ড় is a flap: the tongue curls back and flicks forward, a sound between r and d. Both are written r here. ঢ় is the breathy version (written rh) and is rare.

about.title: Nasal sounds
about.text:
The chondrobindu ( ঁ ) written over a letter means that the vowel is spoken through the nose, as in French 'bon'. It is not a separate n sound. This course writes it as an n after the vowel: চাঁদ chaand (moon), পাঁচ paanch (five), হ্যাঁ hyaan (yes). So an n directly after a vowel and before another consonant in the roman line is often only a nasal colouring - check the Bengali spelling.

Nasalisation carries meaning and respect. তার (taar) is 'his/her'; তাঁর (taanr) is the respectful form. বাধা (baadhaa) is 'obstacle'; বাঁধা (baandhaa) is 'tied'.

The sound ng (as in 'sing') is written with ঙ or with the sign ং: রং rong (colour), বাংলা baanglaa. In ঙ্গ a hard g usually follows the ng. The letter ঞ occurs almost only in the conjuncts ঞ্চ (nch) and ঞ্জ (nj), where it is simply an n.

ণ and ন are both pronounced n in modern Bengali.

about.title: Conjuncts and letters you do not pronounce
about.text:
When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, they are written as one combined shape, a conjunct (juktaakkhor). Many are easy to recognise - the first letter is squeezed on top of or beside the second (স্ত = স + ত, ন্ধ = ন + ধ). A few must be learnt as shapes: ক্ষ (ক + ষ), জ্ঞ (জ + ঞ), ঞ্চ, ঙ্গ, ত্র, ক্র, হ্ম.

Several conjuncts are not pronounced the way they are spelt. These are the ones every reader must know.

ক্ষ is kh at the start of a word and kkh in the middle: ক্ষমা khomaa, শিক্ষক shikkhok. There is no s sound in it.

জ্ঞ is g at the start of a word and gg in the middle, and it often turns a following aa into the vowel of 'cat': জ্ঞান gyaan, বিজ্ঞান biggaan.

য-ফলা ( ্য ), the hook written after a consonant: at the start of a word it is silent or changes the vowel to the 'a' of 'cat' (ব্যথা byathaa, ব্যাগ byaag - the y in the roman line stands for that vowel change). In the middle of a word it doubles the consonant before it: অন্য onno, সত্য shotto, ধন্যবাদ dhonnobaad.

ব-ফলা (a small ব under a consonant) is silent at the start of a word and doubles the consonant in the middle: স্বামী shaamee, জ্বর jor, বিশ্বাস bisshaash. (In ম্ব and in ব্ব the b is real: লম্বা lombaa.)

ম-ফলা behaves the same way in many words: স্মৃতি sriti, পদ্ম poddo, আত্মীয় aatteeyo. (But it is a real m after ন, ণ, ল, ম, ঙ, গ and others: জন্ম jonmo.)

The bishorgo ( ঃ ) in the middle of a word doubles the next consonant: দুঃখ dukkho.

র has two special forms: রেফ, a stroke above the following consonant when r comes first (কর্ম kormo), and র-ফলা, a stroke below when r comes second (প্রথম prothom).

about.title: Different letters, same sound
about.text:
Bengali spelling preserves distinctions from Sanskrit that are no longer spoken. For reading you only need to know that these letters sound alike; for writing, the spelling of each word has to be learnt.

শ, ষ and স are all pronounced sh in native words: শাক shaak, ষাট shaat, সাত shaat. They become a true s only in certain conjuncts - before ত, থ, ন, র, ল (রাস্তা raastaa, স্নান snaan, শ্রী sree, প্রশ্ন prosno) - and in many English loanwords (বাস baas 'bus', সাইজ saaij 'size'). The romanisation shows which is said.

জ and য are both j: জল jol, যাই jaai. The letter য় (with a dot) is different: it is a y-glide between vowels or at the end of a word (সময় shomoy, মেয়ে meye). After ও it sounds like a w, so ওয়া is written owaa: খাওয়া khaaowaa.

ন and ণ are both n. ই / ঈ are both i; উ / ঊ are both u (written i / ee and u / oo here only to mirror the spelling). ত and ৎ are the same t; ৎ is the form used when no vowel follows. ঙ and ং are the same ng.

The vowel এ has two sounds: usually the e of 'bed', but in many common words the a of 'cat' - এক (one), কেন (why), কেমন (how), দেখা (to see), এখন (now), খেলা (to play). The same 'cat' vowel is spelt অ্যা at the start of loanwords (অ্যাম্বুলেন্স). This course writes এ as e in both cases and tells you in a note when it is the 'cat' sound.

examples.english: seven (the letter looks like s, said sh)
I go (the letter y, said j)
one (the e is the a of 'cat')

about.title: The romanisation used in this course
about.text:
The roman line shows how a phrase is pronounced, not how it is spelt letter by letter. It is always in lower case.

Vowels: o = অ (built-in vowel) and ও; aa = আ, the a of 'father'; i = ই and ee = ঈ, both the i of 'machine' said short; u = উ and oo = ঊ, both the u of 'put'; e = এ (see the note on its two sounds); oi = ঐ; ou = ঔ; ri = ঋ. A single a (in ya, yaa, or at the start of a loanword) is the a of 'cat': byaag, hyaan, ambulens. When two vowels stand together, say both: khaai = khaa-i, jaao = jaa-o, dii = di-i.

Consonants: k kh g gh ng; ch chh j jh; t th d dh n (for both the dental and the retroflex rows); p ph b bh m; r (র and ড়), rh (ঢ়), l; sh (শ ষ স), s where a true s is said; h; j also for য; y for য়; w for the glide in ওয়া.

h after a consonant = a puff of breath (kh, gh, chh, jh, th, dh, ph, bh). The one exception is sh.

n after a vowel can be the nasal sign: paanch, hyaan, taanr.

A doubled consonant is held longer: onno, dukkho, bisshaash. The cluster চ্ছ is written chchh (aachchhaa), since chh is already one sound.

The two forms নও ('you are not') and হও ('you become') are written nou and hou; say no-o and ho-o.

The built-in vowel is written only where it is said: naam, gorom, golpo.

about.title: Kolkata and Dhaka
about.text:
This course teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhaashaa) as spoken in Kolkata and West Bengal. It is understood everywhere Bengali is spoken, including Bangladesh, and the grammar and almost all of the vocabulary are shared.

The differences you will notice first are a handful of everyday words. West Bengal says জল (jol) for water, Bangladesh says পানি (paani). Other pairs: নুন / লবণ (salt), স্নান / গোসল (bath), মাংস / গোশত (meat), জলখাবার / নাস্তা (breakfast, snack), নমস্কার / আসসালামু আলাইকুম (greeting), দাদা / ভাই or ভাইয়া (elder brother), দিদি / আপা (elder sister), সঙ্গে / সাথে (with), নেমন্তন্ন / দাওয়াত (invitation). Many of these follow religion as much as geography.

Some verb forms differ slightly: Kolkata prefers the shortened forms taught here (গেছি gechhi, ঘুমোচ্ছে ghumochchhe, তিনটে tinte), where Bangladesh standard prefers the fuller ones (গিয়েছি, ঘুমাচ্ছে, তিনটা).

The unit notes point out the variants that matter. Whichever you use, you will be understood on both sides of the border.

letters.note: The eleven vowels as full letters, used at the start of a word or after another vowel. After a consonant each one (except অ, which is built in) is written as a sign instead - see 'Vowel signs'.

items.note: The vowel built into every consonant. Like the o of 'hot', or a short closed o as in 'go'. Never the a of Hindi.
The a of 'father'.
Called 'short i' (hrossho i). The i of 'machine', said short.
Called 'long i' (deergho ee), but pronounced exactly like ই today.
Called 'short u' (hrossho u). The u of 'put'.
Called 'long u' (deergho oo), but pronounced exactly like উ today.

A glide from o to i, like the oi of 'boil' with a closed o.
Always the closed o of 'go', without the English glide to u.
A glide from o to u, like 'oh' said with rounded lips at the end.

letters.note: Each letter is named and read with its built-in vowel: ক is 'ko'. The first twenty-five are arranged in rows of five by place in the mouth: throat, palate, retroflex, teeth, lips. In each row: plain, breathy, voiced, voiced breathy, nasal.

letters.note: The signs (kaar) that replace the built-in o, shown here on ক. Notice where each one is written: left, right, below or on both sides of the consonant.

items.note: আ-কার, written on the right.
ই-কার, written on the left but spoken after the consonant.
ঈ-কার, written on the right. Sounds the same as ই-কার.
উ-কার, written below. Special shapes: গু gu, রু ru, শু shu, হু hu.
ঊ-কার, written below. Sounds the same as উ-কার. Special shape: রূ roo.
ঋ-কার, written below. Special shape: হৃ hri.
এ-কার, written on the left. In this example the vowel is the a of 'cat'.
ঐ-কার, written on the left.
ও-কার, written on both sides of the consonant.
ঔ-কার, written on both sides of the consonant.

letters.note: Marks that are not full letters: the three traditional signs at the end of the alphabet, the vowel-killer, and the special attached forms of য, র and ব.

items.note: Onusshaar. The ng of 'sing', the same sound as ঙ. Written after the letter it follows.
Bishorgo. In the middle of a word it is not an h: it doubles the following consonant. At the end of an exclamation it is a short breath.
Chondrobindu, shown here on আ. The vowel is spoken through the nose; there is no real n sound.
Hoshonto, the stroke under a letter, removes the built-in vowel. It is seldom seen in print because consonants without a vowel are normally joined into a conjunct instead.
য-ফলা (jo-pholaa), the form of য after a consonant. At the start of a word it gives the a of 'cat'; in the middle it doubles the consonant: অন্য onno.
র-ফলা (ro-pholaa), the form of র after a consonant: a stroke below. Special shapes: ক্র kr, ত্র tr.
রেফ (reph), the form of র before a consonant: a stroke above the letter that is spoken after it.
ব-ফলা (bo-pholaa), a small ব under a consonant. Silent at the start of a word; in the middle it doubles the consonant: বিশ্বাস bisshaash.
